newsitem.title: PERU: Japan pushes cautious approach in Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan pushes cautious approach in Peru crisis.

text.p: Japanese foreign minister Yukihiko Ikeda appeared Friday to be pushing a cautious, go-slow approach to dealings with guerrillas holding about 400 hostages in the residence of Japan's ambassador to Peru.
Ikeda, who dashed to Lima from Tokyo to be Japan's adviser in the multinational crisis, wrapped up nearly 20 hours of non-stop diplomacy on the fourth day of the siege.

In meetings with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, the ambassadors of the United States and Canada and the chief representative of the Red Cross here, Ikeda pressed Tokyo's main point that the top priority was to avoid bloodshed.
Japan has a record of preferring to negotiate its way out of hostage situations, and had indicated it differed sharply with Peru on how to handle the Lima crisis.

U.S. ambassador Dennis Jett told reporters after meeting Ikeda, a close confidant of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, that Washington's priority also was a peaceful solution to the crisis and the preservation of hostages' lives.
Both countries stressed, however, that they would respect Peru's decisions on how to solve the crisis.

Japanese officials kept silent on what was discussed in Ikeda's meetings. But a statement by Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi that he was confident of a peaceful solution appeared to indicate Ikeda's mission had been successful.

Hashimoto sent Ikeda to Peru, with which Tokyo has close links because of Fujimori's Japanese ancestry, with instructions to communicate Japan's position, to meet families of Japanese hostages and Japanese-Peruvian families and to set up a task force in the absence of an ambassador.
